established_findings.statement: LLMs can generate or translate high-level network intents into low-level network configurations in research prototypes and benchmarked/simulated settings.
limitations: Evidence comes from prototypes, benchmarks, or simulation-level studies rather than large-scale production deployments
Reported success often uses curated tasks, limited protocol/vendor coverage, or synthetic inputs

established_findings.statement: Hallucination (plausible but incorrect outputs) is a widely observed failure mode of LLMs and is documented across surveys and empirical studies.
established_findings.evidence_type: Surveys and empirical studies of LLM hallucination
limitations: Surveys synthesize many settings; actual hallucination rates depend strongly on task, prompt, and evaluation methodology relevant to NetOps tasks

established_findings.statement: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), external verification, and generate–verify–repair patterns reduce factual errors in LLM outputs in prior studies and are used as mitigation strategies in NetOps-oriented proposals.
established_findings.evidence_type: Systematic reviews and experimental method papers / applied NetOps prototype
limitations: Effectiveness is task- and implementation-dependent; most evidence is simulation/prototype-level rather than longitudinal production trials
Some evaluations report trade-offs (e.g., latency, complexity) when adding retrieval/verification

established_findings.statement: Deterministic/verifier tools for network-configuration checking (e.g., Batfish) and distributed verifiers (e.g., S2) exist and are used to validate configurations at scale in research.
limitations: Scalability limits remain an active engineering concern for very large service-provider scales (papers report trade-offs and distributed approaches)
Integration between LLM pipeline outputs and such verifiers is demonstrated in prototypes but not proven at production scale

established_findings.statement: Agentic/generate–validate–repair architectures with human-in-the-loop checks and sandbox verification are widely recommended in the NetOps literature as safer deployment patterns.
established_findings.evidence_type: Architectural proposals, position papers, and prototypes
limitations: Recommendations are often based on conceptual architectures and prototypes rather than controlled production deployments
Human-in-the-loop designs vary widely and operator burden/usability is incompletely measured

unresolved_questions.statement: Are LLM-based agents demonstrated (in the supplied records) to safely execute autonomous, unapproved, production network changes at scale? (absence-of-evidence rather than evidence-of-absence)
unresolved_questions.evidence_type: Evidence gap / absence in supplied records
limitations: Supplied records include prototypes, benchmarks, and architectural proposals but do not report validated production deployments showing safe autonomous, unapproved changes

unresolved_questions.statement: Can LLM-only self-correction reliably achieve configuration correctness in NetOps without dependable external verifiers or ground-truth feedback?
unresolved_questions.evidence_type: Mixed-method surveys and experiments on self-correction
limitations: Surveys indicate self-correction often fails unless reliable external feedback is available; domain-specific NetOps evidence is limited

unresolved_questions.statement: Do current NetOps/AIOps benchmarks and simulation-based evaluations predict real-world operational safety and reliability for LLM-driven workflows?
limitations: Analyses warn about synthetic-vs-real gaps and external-validity issues; supplied benchmark papers are useful but limited in scope and deployment realism

unresolved_questions.statement: What are the operational cost/latency trade-offs when adding RAG, verification, and distributed verification into LLM-driven NetOps pipelines at operator-relevant SLAs?
limitations: Some papers report quality–latency trade-offs in retrieval and verification; comprehensive cost/latency evaluations in production-like NetOps SLAs are not supplied

candidate_gaps.statement: No supplied record provides a large-scale, execution-grounded benchmark that couples natural-language intent→configuration generation with sandboxed execution, formal verification traces, and operator-approval workflows end-to-end.
candidate_gaps.evidence_type: Gap inferred from scope of benchmark/prototype papers
limitations: Individual components (intent translation, configuration generation, verification, log analysis) exist in supplied records, but integrated end-to-end benchmarks with execution traces and operator-loop metrics are not shown

candidate_gaps.statement: Public, large-scale datasets of paired real-world intents, device-specific configurations, and verified execution outcomes (including failures/rollbacks) are limited in the supplied records.
limitations: Some benchmarks and data-collection efforts exist, but they appear limited in scale, vendor diversity, and ground-truth execution traces

candidate_gaps.statement: Standardized operational correctness metrics (reachability, isolation, ACL/policy compliance, rollback-safety) tailored to LLM-driven NetOps workflows are underrepresented in the supplied literature.
limitations: Papers advocate workflow-centred evaluation, but consistent metric sets tied to sandboxed execution + verifier outputs are not widely established in the supplied records

candidate_gaps.statement: Domain-specific validation of RAG and self-correction methods for NetOps (i.e., experiments that measure repair-success rates against formal verifiers across diverse topologies/protocols) is limited among supplied records.
limitations: RAG/self-correction evidence is encouraging generally, but direct NetOps-domain validation against formal verifiers and across multi-vendor/device heterogeneity is sparse in the supplied set

excluded_claims: LLMs are production-ready to autonomously perform unapproved network changes at scale (no supplied records provide production-deployment evidence)
Existing NetOps benchmarks conclusively predict safe field deployment of LLM-driven agents (supplied records warn about synthetic-vs-real gaps and limited external validity)
Self-correction by an LLM alone (without reliable external verification) is sufficient to guarantee configuration correctness in NetOps (surveys show limited success without external feedback)
